entries.interest: This is the material-conditional shadow of an axiom that is genuinely contested elsewhere: for `⊃` the schema is a one-line tautology (`q` is either true or false, and either way one disjunct is secured vacuously), but the identically-shaped axiom for a conditional sensitive to non-actual worlds is exactly what divides Stalnaker from Lewis. Stalnaker's logic of conditionals builds it in -- Egré and Rott's survey glosses his system as “C2 with the incorporation of CEM into VC”, i.e. Lewis's own axiomatization plus this one further principle -- while Lewis's official system omits it, because his semantics allows a tie for closest antecedent-world with no fact of the matter about the consequent. So the entry that is trivial here is the fault line there: whether “if the coin had been flipped it would have landed heads, or it would have landed tails” is guaranteed by logic alone, or is a further, deniable assumption about how conditionals work. The derivation earns its `Monster-tier` billing honestly: neither disjunct is dictated by the goal, so the only way in is to prove `q ∨ ∼q` as an undictated lemma first (the same shape as `excluded-middle`) and then split on it -- a proof by cases sitting on top of an undictated reductio, with nothing about the goal telling a student to reach for either.

english.gloss: Either if p then q, or if p then not-q.

appearances.quote: system C2 with the incorporation of CEM into VC is Stalnaker's logic of conditionals.

entries.interest: Among any three sentences, some two agree in truth value -- there are only two values to go around, so three sentences cannot all disagree pairwise. That is Lecture 3's bivalence assumption turned into a theorem-generator: a fact that looks like it needs counting rather than logic turns out to be a clean 8-row tautology once written as `(p ≡ q) ∨ (q ≡ r) ∨ (p ≡ r)`. No source in the imports inventory names a champion for it -- it is a brainstormed candidate, carried here with `appearances_pending` rather than a manufactured citation; a logic textbook's discussion of bivalence as a pigeonhole principle would settle it. The derivation is the longest in the database: three separate `∼∨` lemmas (`p ∨ ∼p`, `q ∨ ∼q`, `r ∨ ∼r`, each proved the `excluded-middle` way) feed a case split that only goes three atoms deep where `p` and `q` actually disagree -- when they already agree the first disjunct settles it on the spot, so the tree is lopsided rather than a uniform eight-way fork.

entries.interest: `self-undermining-conditional` already carries the → half of this -- `p ⊃ ∼p` forces `∼p` on its own, one premise supplying both halves of the contradiction once `p` is assumed. What is easy to miss is that the converse holds too: `∼p` alone is enough to hand back `p ⊃ ∼p` vacuously, so the two are not just co-entailing but classically *identical*. Students expect a conditional that undermines its own antecedent to be paradoxical in the way `the-monster` or the Curry sequent are; classically it just collapses into the negation, no residue left over. This single equivalence covers what PS2.8b and PS4.2b set separately (the table and the tree, on the one-directional form) in one stroke. It is also worth setting beside Aristotle's thesis, `∼(p ⊃ ∼p)` -- a schema connexive logicians take as a law but which is classically *contingent*, equivalent to `p` itself rather than a theorem; the two forms look like mirror images but behave quite differently once you check them against a table.

english.gloss: p implying its own negation is the same as p's negation holding outright.

entries.interest: `p ∨ q` alone -- no second premise -- delivers `∼p ⊃ q`, and the two are truth-functionally equivalent, so the inference runs both ways. That equivalence is what philosophers of conditionals call the direct argument: anyone who accepts that a disjunction licenses the matching conditional is already treating indicative *if* as the material conditional, which most accounts of ordinary conditionals deny. The derivation is not a new idea so much as `disjunctive-syllogism` wearing an extra layer: assume the antecedent `∼p`, and the case split on `p ∨ q` needs exactly that entry's nested reductio to strip the `p` case down to `q`, with the `q` case falling out for free. No source in the imports inventory names a champion for this direction of the inference; a survey of the direct argument in the conditionals literature would settle it.

entries.interest: `curry-complete` runs the paradox on two `⊃` premises, one for contraction and one for the fixed point; this is the same collapse packaged into a single biconditional, and no negation appears anywhere in the seven-line proof -- `≡E`, `⊃I` and `⊃E` are all it needs. A sentence that says 'if I am true, then q' makes q provable outright, whatever q is, and the argument never touches a contradiction, so none of the usual reductio-shaped responses to the Liar apply to it. What the proof does need is `p` in two roles: once as the assumption that unlocks `p ⊃ q` from the biconditional, and again, once that conditional is detached, as the very premise that fires it -- the single reuse that a contraction-free logic is built to refuse. Compare `curry-complete`, which spells the same reuse out across two premises instead of one.

entries.interest: Section 6.5 calls the classical reductio the commonest shape in the database, and this is the shape stripped to its minimum: nearly thirty of the proofs already here end a subproof by pairing this step with its mirror, `NegE`, to strip a double negation back down to the goal -- yet nothing has asked for the step on its own until now. Its own proof needs nothing beyond the reductio's bare skeleton: `p` already supplies one half of the contradiction that `⊥I` needs, so assuming `∼p` and reiterating it into that role is the entire subproof, five lines in total, one of them the premise. That shortness is not a shortcut -- there is no explosion rule among the twelve, so a contradiction never hands over a formula directly, and the reductio has to run even when one side of it was sitting on the page from the start. The result marks the safe edge of the intuitionist boundary: `p ⊢ ∼∼p` holds constructively, while its converse, double-negation elimination, does not.

entries.interest: `constructive-dilemma` is already the course's own worked example (PS1 names it); this is its dual, and the two look like mirror images until the derivation is actually found. Where the constructive form gets its disjuncts by straight `⊃E` -- the case is `p`, the conditional hands back `r`, done -- each case here has to go by reductio: assume the antecedent, derive the consequent, collide with the disjunct that names its negation, and only then discharge to the negative conclusion `⊃I`-style rules do not name. Same shape, same two premises playing the same roles, and yet one is `medium` and the other `hard` -- a clean illustration of §14.3's point that length is not what difficulty tracks.

entries.interest: `⊃` and one designated falsehood are already known to be expressively complete for the classical connectives; this identity is the disjunction case spelled out, and it needs no negation anywhere in either half. The forward direction is a short proof by cases; the reverse is the more interesting one, because `p∨q` is not itself conditional-shaped, so getting it out of `(p⊃q)⊃q` forces an undictated reductio -- assume `∼(p∨q)`, and the two disjuncts' *absence* is what has to do the work, each ruled out in turn before a vacuous `p⊃q` can even be built. `disjunction-as-conditional` trades `∨` for `⊃` and `∼` together; this one spends an extra `q` instead of the negation, which is the more surprising trade.

english.gloss: p or q holds exactly when supposing p implies q is already enough, on its own, to guarantee q.

entries.interest: The same one-line move as `addition` (`p ⊢ p∨q`, `∨I` and nothing else), but read as an instruction rather than a claim, and the innocence disappears. "Post the letter" licenses "post it or burn it" by the same rule that licenses the parallel indicative inference, yet obeying the second permits an act the first forbids. McNamara and Van De Putte's survey of deontic logic calls it the earliest and best known challenge to the principle that `OBp` should entail `OB(p∨q)` -- our entry is the bare propositional skeleton underneath that modal dispute, valid and one line long, exactly like `addition`; the puzzle is entirely about what the imperative or deontic reading of `∨I` is doing that the truth-functional reading is not.

english.gloss: Post the letter; therefore post it or burn it.

appearances.quote: The earliest and most well-known challenge to RM is Ross's Paradox (Ross 1941).

entries.interest: The same monotonicity idea as `antecedent-strengthening`, doubled. That entry pads the antecedent with a fresh conjunct and stops at `q`; this one pads the antecedent *and* loosens the conclusion into a fresh disjunct, so a valid conditional survives being made harder to trigger and easier to satisfy at the same time. The two moves are independent -- `&E` finds `p` inside `p & r`, `∨I` covers `q` with `q ∨ s` -- so the derivation is barely longer than the entry it doubles, one extra line for the disjunction.

entries.interest: Compose two conditionals under one shared antecedent: given `p⊃q`, a proof of `q⊃r` conditional on `p` collapses into a proof of `r` conditional on `p`. It is the self-distribution scheme -- Frege's own axiom, and the S-combinator's shape in propositional dress -- with the outer premise `p⊃q` handed over rather than proved alongside it, which is what keeps this version to two levels of nesting where the unrestricted axiom needs three. `hypothetical-syllogism` chains the same two conditionals as two separate premises; here one link is fixed in advance and the other only appears as a hypothesis nested inside the goal, so the chaining happens inside a single conditional instead of across two.

entries.interest: Exportation, applied twice and reordered. Unfold the premise's antecedent and `p⊃((q&r)⊃s)` becomes `(p&q&r)⊃s`; unfold the conclusion the same way and `(p&r)⊃(q⊃s)` becomes `(p&r&q)⊃s` -- the same three-way conjunction, with `q` and `r` swapped. `exportation` states that unfolding as a biconditional for one conjunction; this is the one-directional inference that falls out of applying it twice while the conjuncts change places, which is exactly why the derivation needs a `&E`/`&I` pair to carry `r` across the conditional that exportation's own proof never has to move.

entries.interest: Restall poses this as a direct challenge inside his own natural-deduction chapter: derive it without appealing to `NegE` itself, and notice that nothing else in the system gets you there -- no combination of the other eleven rules eliminates a double negation. That is exactly why `NegE` is one of the twelve rather than a theorem *of* the twelve, and the entry's own derivation makes the point by being as short as a derivation can be: one line, a single citation of the rule that exists for precisely this move. Its mirror `double-negation-introduction` costs a full reductio -- assume `~p`, reiterate it, collide it with the premise, discharge -- so the two directions of double negation are not symmetric in proof even though they are symmetric in content.

entries.interest: `p ⊃ ∼q` and `q ⊃ ∼p` are not merely equivalent -- they are the same claim twice over, true on exactly the rows where `p` and `q` are not both true. Restall sets this as one of Chapter 7's five sequents provable without double-negation elimination, and the derivation shows why the swap is free: assume `q` toward `∼p`, assume `p` for the reductio, and `⊃E` on the premise hands back `∼q`, which contradicts the still-accessible `q` outright. Nothing here routes through a double negation, which is what separates it from `contraposition-recovered`'s half of ordinary contraposition -- that direction lands on `∼∼q` and has to spend `NegE` to close the last inch, while this one's goal is a bare negation from the first line to the last.

entries.interest: The same Abelian-logic axiom as `abelian-axiom`, with the atom `q` in both positions replaced by `q & r`. The extra conjunct does not change the logical shape -- the countermodel is still the unique row where the inner conditional's consequent is true and `p` is false -- but it takes the table from four rows to eight and gives the tree a genuine second resolution, which is exactly the gap between the parent entry's Lecture 4 table and a Lecture 6 tree worth assigning. Meyer and Slaney's axiom is the converse of Assertion, a classical theorem; adopting it as a schema is what makes a logic Abelian, and here it fails on exactly one row in eight. A clean 'hunt for the single open branch' exercise once three atoms are in play.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `p = F, q = T, r = T`. With `q & r` true, the inner conditional `(p ⊃ (q & r)) ⊃ (q & r)` is true regardless of `p`, so the whole thing collapses to 'therefore `p`' with nothing behind it -- the parent axiom's single failing row, now needing `q` and `r` true together to trigger it.

appearances.locus: in Priest, Routley & Norman (eds.), Paraconsistent Logic: Essays on the Inconsistent (1989)

course.note: Harder partner to `abelian-axiom`: same schema, one substitution, eight rows instead of four. Pairs well as a Lecture 6 tree once the two-atom version has been done as a Lecture 4 table.

nd.note: No derivation; the tree closes on every branch except the one where `q & r` is true and `p` is false.

entries.interest: Boethius' Thesis says a conditional and its opposite-consequent conditional cannot both hold -- 'if p, q' and 'if p, not-q' are supposed to be mutually exclusive, which is exactly how the English conditional feels in use. Classically it fails, and it fails for the reason every connexive thesis fails: when the antecedent is false, both conditionals go true vacuously, so nothing stops them holding together. This instance replaces the antecedent with a conjunction, so the trap now springs whenever `p` and `q` are not *both* true -- six of the eight rows -- rather than on a single false atom. The tree opens fast; the interest is that a student trying ND first will burn real time before Soundness tells them to stop.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Any row where `p & q` is false: with the conjunction false, `(p&q)⊃r` and `(p&q)⊃∼r` are both vacuously true, so the claim that they cannot jointly hold fails outright.

english.gloss: If p and q together guarantee r, then it isn't true that p and q together guarantee not-r.

appearances.work: De Syllogismo Hypothetico (per Kneale & Kneale's reading)

course.note: Instructor-facing attribution note: the Boethius attribution itself is contested (Wansing's SEP article on connexive logic argues the Kneale & Kneale reading of 843D misreads Boethius; see the Comprehensive Logic Inventory §6.5). Safe to teach as 'Boethius' Thesis' by name -- that is the standard label in the connexive-logic literature regardless -- but do not present the attribution to Boethius himself as settled if a student asks.

nd.note: No derivation. The countermodel is any row where `p & q` is false, since then `(p&q)⊃r` and `(p&q)⊃∼r` are both vacuously true and the argument's right-hand side fails -- the same vacuous-truth trap the plain two-atom thesis exhibits, now triggered whenever *either* conjunct fails rather than a single antecedent.

entries.interest: The quantifier-shift fallacy `(∀x)(∃y)Rxy ⊬ (∃x)(∀y)Ryx` -- 'everyone loves someone' does not give you 'someone is loved by everyone' -- with the quantifiers eliminated over a two-element domain `{a, b}`. Restall works this exact tree in *Logic*, Box 9.1 (p. 102). Four atoms and a genuinely hard tree: this previews the second half of the course (quantifiers) from entirely inside propositional logic, since every step a student takes here is a step they will retake, unabbreviated, once `x` and `y` range over more than two things.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `r_aa = T, r_ab = F, r_ba = F, r_bb = T` (and its mirror image): each individual loves only themselves, so everyone loves someone, but no one is loved by both -- neither `a` nor `b` is a shared target.

english.gloss: Everyone loves someone: a loves a or b, and b loves a or b. So someone is loved by everyone: either both love a, or both love b.

course.note: Four atoms, hard tree (2 of 16 rows are countermodels) -- a good bridge exercise right before quantified trees start, since the resolution steps are identical to what `(∀x)(∃y)Rxy` will require once written out unabbreviated.

nd.note: No derivation. The countermodel is exactly the case where the two individuals love different targets -- `a` loves only `a`, `b` loves only `b` -- so ∨-elimination on the premises secures one relation at a time but never both halves of either conjunctive disjunct together.

entries.interest: Aristotle's Second Thesis says one consequent cannot follow both from an antecedent and from its negation -- McCall traces the claim to *Prior Analytics* II.4, 57b3–14, the same stretch that grounds Aristotle's (first) Thesis. The thesis is asserted with formula metavariables, so this instance -- consequent `q & r` rather than a bare atom -- is a straightforward substitution, not a new claim, and stays a theorem in the connexive systems (Wansing's `C` among them) that assert it, since those are closed under substitution like any Hilbert-style system. Classically it fails, and fails for the reason every entry in this family fails: once `q & r` is simply true, both `p ⊃ (q & r)` and `∼p ⊃ (q & r)` go through with `p` doing no work at all, so the 'competing' conditionals were never in competition. Two rows out of eight show it, and both are rows where `q` and `r` are already true before `p` is even asked.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Either row where `q & r` is just true outright: `p ⊃ (q & r)` and `∼p ⊃ (q & r)` both come out true for the same reason, since a true consequent makes any conditional true regardless of the antecedent -- the two conditionals were never actually in tension.

english.gloss: It cannot be that p guarantees q-and-r while not-p guarantees q-and-r just as well.

course.note: Pairs with `boethius-thesis`: same vacuous-antecedent mechanism, different connective skeleton (a negated conjunction of two conditionals here, rather than a conditional between them). Worth setting together once both are in the database.

nd.note: Assume the conjunction and aim for ⊥. Splitting on `p` gets `q & r` out of one conditional or the other by ⊃E, but `q & r` is not a contradiction -- it is exactly what the countermodel rows have in common -- so the reductio has nothing to close on.

entries.interest: Abelard's First Principle says one and the same antecedent cannot entail a proposition and its negation both -- Christopher Martin's reading of the *Dialectica* is the standard source (his 'Logic', in *The Cambridge Companion to Abelard*, pp. 158–199), and Angell and Routley later gave the same schema other names ('subjunctive contrariety', 'Strawson's Thesis') without crediting Abelard. This instance puts a disjunction in the antecedent, so falsifying the principle needs the *disjunction* false, not just one disjunct -- a step students routinely skip, since `p ∨ q` reads as easy to make true. Classically the principle fails wherever `p ∨ q` is false: both conditionals go vacuously true, and the 'one antecedent, two contrary consequents' worry evaporates because there was no live antecedent to begin with. It is the same substitution move as `boethius-thesis` and `aristotle-second-thesis`, and, like them, stays a theorem in the connexive systems that assert it, since the schema is closed under substitution.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Either row where `p` and `q` are both false: the disjunction `p ∨ q` is false, so `(p∨q)⊃r` and `(p∨q)⊃∼r` are both vacuously true whatever `r` is -- the principle only ever needs the antecedent falsified, not the two consequents reconciled.

english.gloss: It cannot be that p-or-q guarantees r while also guaranteeing not-r.

appearances.work: Dialectica, per Christopher J. Martin's 'Logic', in The Cambridge Companion to Abelard (2004)

course.note: Pairs with `boethius-thesis` and `aristotle-second-thesis`: same vacuous-antecedent mechanism, this time needing a disjunction falsified rather than a bare atom or a conjunction. The three make a clean 'spot the antecedent' set once all three are in the database.

nd.note: Assume the conjunction and aim for ⊥, by way of `p ∨ q`: once that is available, ⊃E fires on both conditionals at once and `r` clashes with `∼r`. But nothing hands you `p ∨ q` -- it is a disjunction, not a premise -- and the countermodel is exactly the row where it is false, so the reductio never gets the trigger it needs.

entries.interest: The vacuous-truth trap that makes Boethius' Thesis fail, one level of nesting deeper: instead of flipping the whole consequent, the inner conditional's own consequent is flipped, so the claim is that `p` cannot commit `q` to both `r` and `∼r`. This is not a literal substitution instance of Boethius' Thesis -- the genuine nested version would negate `q ⊃ r` outright rather than swap `r` for `∼r` inside it, and those are different formulas -- so no connexive verdict is claimed here, only the family resemblance. Classically the mechanism is the same one three times over: whenever `p` is false, or `p` is true and `q` is false, both `p ⊃ (q ⊃ r)` and `p ⊃ (q ⊃ ∼r)` go through vacuously, so six of the eight rows are countermodels rather than the two or six of its shallower cousins. The bookkeeping is the real difficulty here -- tracking which half of the tree has actually reached a contradiction two levels down.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Any row where `p` is false, or `p` is true and `q` is false: either way the inner conditional's antecedent never gets asked to do anything, so `p ⊃ (q ⊃ r)` and `p ⊃ (q ⊃ ∼r)` both come out true for the same vacuous reason, twice over.

english.gloss: Suppose p guarantees that q guarantees r. Then p cannot also guarantee that q guarantees not-r.

appearances.work: De Syllogismo Hypothetico (per Kneale & Kneale's reading)

course.note: Not a genuine substitution instance of `boethius-thesis` -- see `interest` -- so teach it as a cousin, not as 'Boethius again'. Good next step after `boethius-thesis` once nesting, rather than the vacuous-truth mechanism itself, is the point.

nd.note: From the premise and the assumption `p ⊃ (q ⊃ ∼r)`, getting `r` and `∼r` to clash needs `p` and `q` both established, so that ⊃E can fire on each conditional twice. But nothing in the premise or the assumption hands you `p` or `q` -- both are conditionals with nothing to trigger them -- and the six countermodels are exactly the rows where that trigger is missing.

entries.interest: John McCarthy introduced the qualification problem to name exactly this gap: commonsense generalisations like 'birds fly' carry an open-ended list of unstated exceptions -- injured, oiled, caged, a penguin -- and no finite list of qualifications ever closes it off. Written out as `(b & ∼a_b) ⊃ f, b ⊢ f`, the missing premise is compressed into a single letter, `a_b`, standing for whatever exception is in play; the tree's one open branch is the row where that letter is true and the inference the naive reader wants simply fails to fire. It is the same shape as any suppressed-premise argument, aimed at exactly the intuition -- that an ordinary generalisation licenses its instances -- that motivated non-monotonic logic in the first place.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `b = T, a_b = T, f = F`: it is a bird, but abnormal -- a penguin, an ostrich, one with a broken wing -- and it does not fly. `a_b` is never ruled out by anything actually said.

english.gloss: If something is a bird and nothing is abnormal about it, it flies. This is a bird. So it flies.

course.note: Three atoms, and `a_b` stands in for an open-ended list of exceptions -- a natural pair with any non-monotonic-logic aside in Lecture 7/8.

nd.note: Assume `∼f` and aim at `⊥`. `⊃E` on the first premise needs `b & ∼a_b`, and the only premise about `b` gives `b` alone -- nothing ever produces `∼a_b`, and no other rule can manufacture it. The open branch is exactly the row where `a_b` holds and the qualification is never discharged.

entries.interest: Arthur Prior labelled two rival ways of evaluating future-tense claims over branching time 'Peircean' and 'Ockhamist', naming the first after Peirce's own resistance to a single, already-settled future. Under Peircean semantics, 'it will be that things are thus, or it will be that they are not' can hold on every individual history -- each branch is itself bivalent about how it turns out -- without holding necessarily, across all of them at once: one history can settle for the affirmative, another for the negative, and nothing forces them to agree. Written with `f`/`g` for 'will be thus' and 'will be otherwise' at each of two histories, the two open branches are exactly the two ways the histories can disagree. A clean object lesson in why necessity does not distribute over disjunction: `□(A ∨ B)` does not give you `□A ∨ □B`, whatever the modality.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `f_1 = T, g_1 = F, f_2 = F, g_2 = T`: the first history settles the affirmative, the second settles the negative. Excluded middle held on each history taken alone; nothing tied the two together.

english.gloss: At the first way the future could go, it will be that things are thus or it will be that they are not; and the same at the second way the future could go. So either both ways agree it will be thus, or both agree it will not.

appearances.work: the 'Peircean' semantics for future contingents (the label is Arthur Prior's, for a picture of branching time Prior traced to Peirce)

course.note: Four atoms via the two-history expansion (`X1`/`X2` for 'X at history 1/2'); a good pair with any Lecture 7/8 aside on modal distribution failures.

nd.note: `∨E` on the first premise forces a case split into `f_1` and `g_1`, and inside each case the second premise `f_2 ∨ g_2` still has to be split again with no way to control which disjunct it resolves to -- nothing in either premise ties history 1's outcome to history 2's. The two branches that stay open are exactly the two ways they can come apart.

entries.interest: Johan van Benthem's work on the logic of preference distinguishes a goodness-based reading of 'x is better than y' from a badness-based one, and the two are not simply interchangeable: something can fail to be good without being bad, so a comparison stated one way need not match the same comparison stated the other. Written as a single biconditional over four sentence letters -- one per predicate-object pairing -- the claim that the two readings always coincide is falsifiable in six of its sixteen rows, exactly where the goodness and badness facts about `x` and `y` come apart. A tidy 'these look like the same claim' exercise: nothing about the predicate-logic dressing (`g_x`, `b_y`, and so on) does any work once it is unpacked into four atoms.
entries.countermodel_gloss: `g_x = T, g_y = T, b_y = T, b_x = F`: x and y are both good, so the goodness-based reading has nothing to say about which is preferable -- but y is also bad and x is not, and the badness-based reading declares x the winner anyway.

english.gloss: x is good and y is not, exactly when y is bad and x is not.

appearances.work: van Benthem's work on the logic of preference

course.note: Premise-less, single-formula table layout; four atoms, no nesting -- an easy table and tree, good as a first 'looks valid, isn't' theorem alongside the course's own.

nd.note: There are no premises to work from, so proving the biconditional would need `g_x & ∼g_y` derivable from nothing together with `b_y & ∼b_x` from nothing, in both directions -- and no rule ever fires without a premise or an assumption to feed it. The falsifying rows are exactly where the four atoms are free to come apart.

entries.interest: The material-conditional skeleton of what the literature on conditionals calls a Sobel sequence, after Howard Sobel: a first conditional ('if p, q') undercut by a second, more specific one ('if p and r, not-q'). The tempting move is to blame `r` itself and conclude it can never obtain -- "the defeater never actually obtains" -- but that step needs `p` confirmed first. Both countermodels have `p` false, where each conditional holds vacuously and `r` is left free; the premises alone pin down only that `p` and `r` cannot both hold (`∼(p & r)`, the valid twin drawn from the very same two premises), never that `r` on its own is false. Sobel's own sequences are counterfactual, built to motivate non-monotonic revision as the conversational context shifts from one conditional to the next; the material conditional here can only stage the shape of that puzzle, not its content, since `⊃` has no context left to revise.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Both countermodels make `p` false: once the antecedent never triggers, `p ⊃ q` and `(p & r) ⊃ ∼q` are both true whatever `r` is, so nothing pins `r` down at all. What the premises actually rule out is `p` and `r` holding together, not `r` on its own.

english.gloss: If p, then q. But if p together with r, then not q -- so r must not be the case.

appearances.work: an unpublished manuscript, as reported by David Lewis

course.note: Pairs thematically with `antecedent-strengthening` (`p⊃q ⊨ (p&r)⊃q`, valid): that entry shows the material conditional survives strengthening the antecedent, and this one shows a naive student move that tries to read more into a strengthened antecedent's failure than the logic licenses. Different schema, so no `looks_like`.

nd.note: Wanting `∼r` from the two conditionals needs `p` established, so that `⊃E` can fire on the second premise and force a clash with the first; nothing here hands you `p`, and both countermodels are exactly the rows where `p` fails and the premises are satisfied vacuously, leaving `r` unconstrained.

names: Theological fatalism minus the necessity of the past

entries.interest: The classical theological-fatalism chain runs: God foreknew that X would happen (`k`), so X was true (`t`, from `k ⊃ t`); a true past fact is a necessary one (`n`, from the extra premise this entry omits, `t ⊃ n`); and whatever is necessary is not free (from `n ⊃ ∼f`). Drop that missing link and the chain does not close: the single open branch is `k=T, t=T, n=F, f=T` -- knowledge and truth about the past, without necessity, and freedom intact. That branch *is* William of Ockham's own way out of the argument, the medieval 'Ockhamist' solution to the problem of divine foreknowledge: a past truth that depends on how the future turns out is a *soft* fact rather than a *hard* one, and only hard facts about the past inherit its necessity. Restore `t ⊃ n` -- exactly the fatalist's own extra premise -- and every branch closes.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The one open branch has `k`, `t` and `f` all true and `n` alone false: God knew, it happened, and it still wasn't necessary. That is Ockham's soft-fact move made into a row -- truth about the past is not by itself enough to force necessity.

english.gloss: God knew it. Knowing entails its being true. And whatever is necessary isn't free. So: it wasn't free.

appearances.work: Predestination, God's Foreknowledge, and Future Contingents (his Tractatus de Praedestinatione et de Praescientia Dei respectu Futurorum Contingentium, c. 1321-23; trans. Marilyn McCord Adams and Norman Kretzmann)
appearances.locus: on the distinction between hard and soft facts about the past

course.note: 'Ockhamist' here is the modern label from the analytic philosophy-of-religion debate (via Adams and Kretzmann's translation) for Ockham's own hard-fact/soft-fact distinction, not a quotation from the Latin text -- some readers argue the modern reconstruction only loosely matches Ockham's own argument, flagged rather than overclaimed, the same way `boethius-thesis`'s course.note flags its own contested reading.

nd.note: Getting `∼f` needs `n`, and `n` only arrives by `⊃E` on `n ⊃ ∼f`, which needs `n` already established; the only route to `n` from the other two premises is the missing `t ⊃ n` bridge. Without it, `k` and `k ⊃ t` hand you `t` and nothing further.

entries.interest: George Boole's algebra of logic reads conjunction as multiplication, and his method for solving a logical problem was to write it as an equation, solve the equation exactly as ordinary algebra would, and translate the solution back into logic. `(p & q) ≡ (p & r)` looks exactly like `pq = pr`, and ordinary algebra cancels the `p` to get `q = r` -- but classical propositional logic has no such cancellation law, and the schema is invalid. Both countermodels have `p` false, where `p & q` and `p & r` both collapse to false regardless of `q` and `r`, so the biconditional holds vacuously while `q` and `r` are free to disagree. Boole found the defect himself: ordinary division has no general logical interpretation, which is exactly what motivated the Development, or Expansion, Theorem of *Laws of Thought* -- expand, don't divide.
entries.countermodel_gloss: Both countermodels make `p` false: `p & q` and `p & r` are then both false regardless of `q` and `r`, so the premise holds vacuously while `q` and `r` are free to disagree. What looks like a shared factor to cancel is really a shared way of being vacuously satisfied.

english.gloss: p-and-q holds exactly when p-and-r does. So: q holds exactly when r does.

appearances.work: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought
appearances.locus: Ch. II §14 (division has no general logical interpretation); Ch. V (the Development/Expansion theorem supplied in its place)

course.note: The temptation is literally arithmetical: `(p & q) ≡ (p & r)` reads like `pq = pr`, and cancelling `p` is exactly the move Boole's own algebra could not license in general -- see Theodore Hailperin, 'Boole's Algebra Isn't Boolean Algebra', Mathematics Magazine 54(4) (1981), 61-77, on the missing division law. A good pairing with any aside on why `&` is not literal multiplication despite the notation.

nd.note: Wanting `q` out of the biconditional needs `p` established first, so that eliminating it from both sides would even make sense; nothing in the single premise hands you `p`, and the two countermodels are exactly the rows where `p` fails and the premise is satisfied for a reason that has nothing to do with `q` and `r` agreeing.

Doxastic closure under conjunction elimination, hyperintensional failure

entries.interest: Closure -- believing `p & q` should hand you belief in `p` -- is valid whenever every world the agent takes seriously is a normal, classical one, since `&E` never fails there. Rantala's repair for logical omniscience adds one further, *impossible* world where complex formulas get an arbitrary truth value instead of the one their parts compute, exactly the way SEP §5.3 describes Rantala's own semantics: at a non-normal world a negation gets a truth value independent of what it negates. Render `Bp&q` as "`p&q` holds at every accessible world" and the impossible world's verdict on `p&q` becomes a fresh atom with no route back to `p` and `q` separately -- so `p_2`, the impossible world's verdict on bare `p`, is free to disagree. This is the canonical hyperintensional invalidity, and it fails for a different reason than `doxastic-closure`'s does: there the belief atom is sealed off from its contents entirely, with no internal structure to a truth-functional connective to speak of; here the failure is localised to one impossible alternative, where the connectives still apply everywhere else.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The impossible world is drawable: a normal world where `p` and `q` are both true, sitting beside an impossible one where `p` is stipulated false even though the fresh atom standing for `p&q` there is stipulated true anyway.

appearances.work: Impossible world semantics and logical omniscience (Acta Philosophica Fennica 35, 1982), as reported in Francesco Berto and Mark Jago's SEP entry 'Impossible Worlds'

course.note: Four atoms via the two-world impossible-worlds expansion (`p_1`/`q_1`/`p_2` for "p/q at world 1" and "p at world 2", `c` a fresh atom for the impossible world's verdict on `p&q`); pairs with `doxastic-closure` as a contrast in *how* closure fails -- there the belief atom is sealed off from its contents entirely, here the failure is localised to one impossible alternative.

nd.note: Assume `(p_1 & q_1) & c` and aim for `p_1 & p_2`. `&E` twice gets `p_1` immediately -- the first conjunct is no trouble at all. But nothing links `c` to `p_2`: `c` is a bare atom standing in for the impossible world's arbitrary verdict on `p & q`, and no rule unpacks an atom into a claim about `p` alone. The derivation reaches `p_1` and stalls exactly where the countermodel says it must -- `c` and `p_2` vary independently.

english.gloss: She believes that p and q -- true at every world she takes seriously -- so she believes that p.

entries.interest: Frege's own puzzle, made fully propositional: `h_1 ≡ p_1` says the identity holds at the actual world only, `h_1 & h_2` says she believes `h` -- "Hesperus is bright", say -- at every world she takes seriously, and the question is whether she thereby believes `p`, "Phosphorus is bright", too. It does not follow, and SEP puts the case in the same terms Frege used: someone can know that the morning star is seen near sunrise without thereby knowing that Venus is, exactly because nothing yet says the two names pick out one thing. Fitting's §2.4 gives Marcus's repair in the same breath: make the identity necessary rather than actual -- add `h_2 ≡ p_2` -- and the argument goes through, since now every world she considers has the two propositions rising and falling together. One added biconditional is the entire distance between Frege's puzzle and Marcus's answer to it.
entries.countermodel_gloss: A drawable epistemic model: one world where Hesperus and Phosphorus coincide (the actual world, where the identity was stipulated), and one she also considers possible where they have quietly come apart.

appearances.work: the puzzle of informative identity statements (the morning star and the evening star), rendered as a two-world epistemic model in Melvin Fitting's SEP entry 'Intensional Logic'
appearances.locus: §2.1 (the puzzle) and §2.4 (Ruth Barcan Marcus's necessity-of-identity reply)

course.note: Four atoms via the two-world epistemic expansion (`h_1`/`p_1` at the actual world, `h_2`/`p_2` at the alternative); pairs with `peircean-future-excluded-middle` and `belief-closure-impossible-world` as a family of two-world modal/epistemic expansions, and its own valid twin (add `h_2 ≡ p_2`) is not in the database -- worth setting alongside it as a one-premise contrast.

nd.note: Assume `h_1 ≡ p_1` and `h_1 & h_2`, aim for `p_1 & p_2`. `&E` on the second premise gets `h_1`, then `≡E` on the first gets `p_1` -- the first conjunct is free. But nothing licenses `p_2`: the biconditional was only ever asserted at world 1, and `h_2` alone has no rule connecting an `h`-atom to a `p`-atom at world 2. The derivation reaches `p_1` and stalls exactly where a second biconditional, `h_2 ≡ p_2` -- Marcus's repair -- would close it.

english.gloss: Hesperus is Phosphorus, and she believes -- at every world she takes seriously -- that Hesperus is bright; so she believes that Phosphorus is bright.

names: Löb's axiom with the conclusion unboxed

entries.interest: Löb's axiom, ☐(☐A⊃A)⊃☐A, is GL's defining axiom -- Verbrugge's SEP entry introduces exactly this schema in §2.1, and it is the modal-logic register of Löb's theorem, the formalised reason a system cannot prove its own "if provable then true" without triviality. Expanded on a four-world converse-well-founded chain, where `☐X` at each world unpacks to `X` conjoined across every later world and comes out vacuously true at the endpoint, the genuine axiom is a three-atom tautology whose proof is the well-foundedness argument in miniature: `p_4` from the endpoint, `p_3` by `⊃E`, `p_2` by `&I` and `⊃E`. This entry swaps the boxed conclusion `p_2 & p_3 & p_4` for the bare `p_1` -- "A holds at world 1" rather than "☐A holds at world 1" -- which is exactly the claim GL's own reflection principle, `☐A⊃A`, is built to reject. The single countermodel shows the chain doing everything it can: it fully supports `p_2`, `p_3` and `p_4`, and still leaves `p_1` open, because the box in the conclusion was never optional.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The chain gives every reason to believe the boxed claim two steps up (`p_2`, `p_3` and `p_4` all come out true) and none at all to believe the unboxed claim at world 1 itself.

appearances.work: Löb's axiom for the provability logic GL, ☐(☐A⊃A)⊃☐A, as formalised in Rineke Verbrugge's SEP entry 'Provability Logic'

course.note: Four atoms via the four-world converse-well-founded GL chain (`p_1`…`p_4` for "A at world 1…4"); premise-less, single-formula table layout. Pairs with `hesperus-phosphorus-belief` and `peircean-future-excluded-middle` as a family of multi-world modal expansions, and with the genuine Löb theorem (not yet in the database) as a "drop the box" contrast.

nd.note: Assume the antecedent `((p_3 & p_4) ⊃ p_2) & (p_4 ⊃ p_3) & p_4` and aim for `p_1`. `&E` gets `p_4` outright, `⊃E` on `p_4 ⊃ p_3` gets `p_3`, and `&I` with `⊃E` on the first conjunct gets `p_2` -- the well-founded chain climbs cleanly to `p_2 & p_3 & p_4`, which is the genuine Löb conclusion. But that is a claim about worlds 2 through 4, not world 1, and nothing in the premises says anything about `p_1` at all; the derivation has everything except the one atom it was asked for.

english.gloss: Something could have been F. So something that already exists could have been F.

entries.interest: The formula named for Ruth Barcan Marcus, rendered on a frame whose domain grows: world 1 has only `a`, world 2 gains `b`. The antecedent is `◇∃xFx` read across both worlds -- `a_1∨a_2∨b_2` -- and the consequent is `∃x◇Fx` read against world 1's own domain -- `a_1∨a_2`, the only two atoms naming something that exists there. The single countermodel has `b_2` alone true: something newly existing can possibly be `F` without anything among what already exists being possibly `F`, because the witness the consequent asks for is not there yet to ask about. Three atoms, one open branch, and the whole metaphysical stake of the Barcan formula -- whether possibility ever outruns what actually exists -- sits in that one row.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The domain growing, made visible: at world 1 only `a` exists and it is not `F`; at world 2 the newly-existing `b` is `F`. Nothing at world 1 can serve as the witness the consequent asks for, because it is not there yet to ask about.

appearances.locus: Journal of Symbolic Logic 11 (1946), pp. 1–16 -- the paper introducing the axiomatic system in which the formula bearing her name is derivable

course.note: Two-world domain-expansion rendering: `a_1`/`a_2` for "a is F" at worlds 1/2, `b_2` for "b is F" at world 2 (b does not exist at world 1, so there is no `b_1`).

nd.note: Assume the antecedent `(a_1∨a_2)∨b_2` and aim for `a_1∨a_2`. `∨E` splits into three cases: the `a_1` and `a_2` cases each close immediately by `∨I`, but the `b_2` case has nothing to work with -- `b_2` is a bare atom with no rule connecting it to `a_1` or `a_2`. The derivation stalls exactly there, which is the whole content of the countermodel: the case that stays open is the one the domain grew to allow.

english.gloss: She believes p implies q, and she believes p. So she believes q.

entries.interest: The K axiom -- believing `p⊃q` and believing `p` should hand you belief in `q` -- rendered the way `belief-closure-impossible-world` renders conjunction elimination: one further, impossible world where a complex formula's truth is a fresh atom instead of the value its parts compute. Here it is the conditional's turn: `k` stands for the impossible world's arbitrary verdict on `p⊃q`, while `p_1`, `q_1`, `p_2`, `q_2` keep their ordinary atomic behaviour at both worlds. Belief in `p` carries the normal world's `q_1` out by `⊃E`, but `k` has no route back to `q_2` -- the impossible world's opinion of the whole conditional is severed from what it says about `q` alone. This is `doxastic-closure`'s K-axiom failure again, but with the belief operator's internal structure restored everywhere except the single non-normal alternative that keeps the agent short of logical omniscience.
entries.countermodel_gloss: The impossible world agrees with the normal one about `p` and `q` separately, but is stipulated to make the conditional `p⊃q` true on its own terms rather than by computing it from `p` and `q` there -- so `q` can fail at that world even though the conditional the agent believes says it should not.

appearances.work: Impossible world semantics and logical omniscience (Acta Philosophica Fennica 35, 1982), as reported in Francesco Berto and Mark Jago's SEP entry 'Impossible Worlds'
appearances.locus: §5.3, Impossible Worlds in Epistemic Logic (the K / closure-under-entailment case)

course.note: Five atoms via the two-world impossible-worlds expansion (`p_1`/`q_1`/`p_2`/`q_2` for "p/q at world 1/2", `k` a fresh atom for the impossible world's verdict on `p⊃q`); pairs with `belief-closure-impossible-world` (CLI-140, the same table's Closure row) and `doxastic-closure` as a third telling of logical omniscience.

nd.note: Assume both premises and aim for `q_1&q_2`. `&E` on the first premise gets `p_1⊃q_1` and `k`; `&E` on the second gets `p_1` and `p_2`; `⊃E` on `p_1⊃q_1` and `p_1` gets `q_1` -- the first conjunct of the goal is free. But nothing links `k` or `p_2` to `q_2`: `k` is a bare atom standing for the impossible world's arbitrary verdict on the whole conditional, and `p_2` says only that `p` holds at the second world, with no conditional there to detach anything from. The derivation reaches `q_1` and stalls exactly where the countermodel says it must -- `q_2` is free to vary independently.

entries.interest: The unrestricted self-distribution scheme -- Frege's own axiom (Begriffsschrift, 1879, Proposition 2), and the S combinator's shape in propositional dress. `self-distribution-premised` proves the same collapse with `p⊃q` handed over as a premise, which is what keeps that version to two levels of nesting; here nothing is handed over, so the middle conditional has to be assumed and discharged in its own turn, and the derivation nests three subproofs deep. Together with `K` -- `⊢ p⊃(q⊃p)`, the closed form of `positive-paradox`'s premised sequent -- this axiom proves the Deduction Theorem: every appeal to modus ponens inside a hypothetical proof compiles into one instance of it.

course.note: Unrestricted three-level form of `self-distribution-premised`; the axiom's premised sequent (`p⊃q ⊢ (p⊃(q⊃r))⊃(p⊃r)`) is already in the database, and `K`'s own closed form (`⊢ p⊃(q⊃p)`) is already there too as `positive-paradox`'s premised sequent (`p ⊢ q⊃p`) -- neither needed reimporting.

entries.interest: Jean Nicod's 1917 paper cut *Principia Mathematica*'s propositional logic to one axiom and one rule of inference, both written in the Sheffer stroke -- an entire logic run through a single primitive step. Unfolded into `&` and `∼`, the second premise here is `∼(a & ∼(b & c))`, and that is just `a ⊃ (b & c)` wearing stroke clothing: `∼(X & ∼Y)` is the ordinary equivalence for a conditional. So Nicod's rule does modus ponens and conjunction elimination in one primitive step where our twelve rules need two, which is why the derivation below has to build `a & ∼(b & c)` as a single formula and set it against the second premise directly, rather than detaching `b & c` and then peeling off `c`. The table's numbers say the same thing more starkly: the argument is premise-true on exactly one of its eight rows, the row where `a`, `b` and `c` are all true, which is the only place a conditional and its antecedent can both hold.

appearances.work: A Reduction in the Number of the Primitive Propositions of Logic
appearances.locus: 1917, the paper's single rule of inference

course.note: A clean single-primitive-rule example for a proof-theory aside; the second premise reads as opaque until `∼(a & ∼X)` is pointed out as `a ⊃ X` in disguise.

english.gloss: Take q, whatever it may be. It follows that p, or not p.

entries.interest: Buridan's *Treatise on Consequences* states, alongside its more famous sibling that anything follows from the impossible, that whatever is necessary follows from anything at all. This is the schema that principle licenses: `p ∨ ∼p` is a tautology, so it can be validly inferred from any premise whatever, and here the premise is an arbitrary `q`. The derivation below makes the point sharply -- it is `excluded-middle`'s own reductio with one extra premise line bolted on the front, and `q` is never cited anywhere in the ten lines that follow it, which is exactly what 'follows from anything' should look like on the page. Relevance logicians reject the schema for the same reason: a proof that never touches its premise is not tracking any connection between what is assumed and what is concluded.

appearances.quote: the necessary follows from anything

course.note: Pairs with `excluded-middle`: same tautology, but with a premise attached that the derivation never has to touch. Good for making 'valid' and 'relevant' come apart out loud.

entries.interest: The same passage of Buridan's *Treatise on Consequences* that licenses `necessarium-ad-quodlibet` opens with the sibling principle: anything follows from an impossibility. This is its sharpest instance -- not just any conclusion, but a full contradiction, doubling the explosion. It sits beside `ex-falso` as the same principle in a different shape: there the contradictory halves arrive pre-conjoined in one premise and the conclusion is a bare atom; here they are two separate premises and the conclusion is itself contradictory, so the derivation below proves `q` and `∼q` independently, by the same reductio run twice, and joins them with one final `&I`. It is vacuously valid -- the premises are satisfiable in none of the four rows, so there is no row left over for a countermodel to occupy.

appearances.quote: from the impossible anything follows

course.note: Pairs with `ex-falso` as the same principle in a different shape -- separate premises rather than one conjoined, and a contradictory conclusion rather than an arbitrary one. Good for showing the reductio pattern is reusable, not a one-off trick.

entries.interest: This is the whole rule laid bare: from any premises whatever, an extra one costs nothing. The table shows why -- `q` is idle on every row, true or false, and the argument's validity never consults it. That is exactly the feature relevance logicians single out: SEP's *Logical Consequence* article states the objection to weakening as "the extra premise A need not be used in the derivation of the conclusion C and hence, that C does not follow from the premises X,A in the appropriate sense," and relevant logics are built to do without the rule for that reason. Classically the objection has no force -- an argument with true premises and a false conclusion is what invalidity means, and `p, q ⊢ p` can never have that shape -- but the rejection is not a mistake about validity, it is a different question about what a premise is for.

appearances.who: Jc Beall, Greg Restall & Gil Sagi
appearances.quote: the extra premise A need not be used in the derivation of the conclusion C and hence, that C does not follow from the premises X,A in the appropriate sense

course.note: The shortest entry in the set by every measure -- three-line proof, one derived line, no subproof. Good as the first example when introducing the twelve rules: `Reit` earns its keep here rather than being decoration.

entries.interest: Anderson and Belnap's system E of relevant entailment takes this as one of its axioms, labelled EntT. It is a theorem of classical logic too -- the table below is unanimous -- so nothing about its truth value marks it as belonging to a nonclassical system. What marks it is where it sits in E's own list of axioms: R, the more permissive system of relevant implication built alongside E, states Identity, Suffixing, Assertion, Contraction and the rest, but EntT is not among them. A theorem this shape can hold in a system without being one of its axioms, of course, but the choice to make it primitive in E and not in R is part of what keeps the two systems distinct -- E is meant to be entailment under necessity, R only relevant implication, and EntT is doing some of the work of enforcing that difference.

appearances.who: Alan Ross Anderson & Nuel D. Belnap Jr.

appearances.locus: 1975, the axiomatisation of the system E

entries.interest: `double-negation-elimination` is the one-line argument `∼∼p ⊢ p`; this is its deduction-theorem shadow, `⊢ ∼∼p ⊃ p`, and the two proofs show exactly what the theorem costs beyond the rule -- one `CondI` wrapped around the same single citation of `NegE`. Both fail intuitionistically, and the reason is the same reason in both cases: on the BHK reading a proof of `∼∼p` is a construction that refutes every refutation of `p`, and that is weaker than a construction of `p` itself. Refuting the refutations is not the same as having the thing. Peirce's Law fails intuitionistically too, but its formula has no `∼` in it at all, so it cannot be the clean case for what negation is doing wrong. This one can: the failing connective is sitting right in the formula.

appearances.quote: the classical law of double negation elimination: ¬¬A → A

course.note: Pairs with `double-negation-elimination`: same rule, argument form vs. conditional form. Good for making the deduction theorem visible as a move rather than a slogan -- literally one more line.

entries.interest: The redundant disjunct is the one built entirely from what the other two already share: `q&r` looks like a genuine third case, but between `p` and `~p` the first two disjuncts already cover it. Archie Blake noticed the shape in his 1937 dissertation on the Blake canonical form; Samson and Mills rediscovered it independently in 1954; and it was W. V. Quine, in 1955, who gave it the name it now carries -- "consensus". (Repeated consensus is also one algorithm for computing that canonical form, and John Alan Robinson generalised the move to clausal logic in 1965 as the resolution rule.) The derivation earns the asymmetry honestly: going from `(p&q)|(~p&r)` to the full three-way disjunction is one line, since a true disjunct is still true with a third one added; the other direction needs a full case split on `q&r`, and the hard case nests four subproofs deep -- assuming the whole two-way disjunction false, then a reductio for each of its two disjuncts, then a reductio for `p` itself -- before a direct `ConjI` builds the second disjunct outright and collides it with what the reductios already ruled out.

english.gloss: 'You're seated if it's a weekday and you booked ahead, or it isn't a weekday and you're on the walk-in list, or you booked ahead and you're on the walk-in list' says just what 'you're seated if it's a weekday and you booked ahead, or it isn't a weekday and you're on the walk-in list' says -- the third case never adds a seat the first two didn't already give you.

entries.interest: Y's own missing type, made propositional. `Yx ▷ x(Yx)` sends an `A⊃A` to an `A`, so `Y`'s type would have to be `(A⊃A)⊃A` -- and that schema alone is not a theorem (`⊢(p⊃p)⊃p` fails at `p=F`, per §2.17b's own table). Hand in the one thing every instance of `A⊃A` already provides for free, though, and the schema turns trivial: from `p⊃p` and `(p⊃p)⊃p` together, `p` is one step of ⊃E away. `derive.py`'s own premise_analysis confirms the first premise does no work here -- the argument stays valid with `p⊃p` dropped, since `(p⊃p)⊃p` alone already agrees with `p` on every row of its own table. "Every function has a fixed point" has an exact propositional shadow, and per Bimbó's SEP entry, the shadow is triviality.

entries.interest: The propositional shadow of Vann McGee's 1985 "A Counterexample to Modus Ponens" -- and shadow is the operative word. Read `⊃` as material and this is nothing but a nested modus ponens, six lines end to end; `derive.py` confirms exactly 3 of the 8 rows keep both premises true, and the conclusion is true on every one of those three -- no countermodel, no surprise. McGee's actual target is the *indicative* conditional under a probabilistic semantics, where both premises can be highly credible while the conclusion is not; that failure needs probability, exactly as the row's own note says, not truth-functional composition. Read as a felt counterexample to ⊃-elimination, the propositional fragment is precisely where the puzzle disappears -- Edgington's own SEP survey walks through the Reagan-election scenario that makes the case (§5).

entries.interest: The material conditional makes this a one-line triviality -- `q` follows from `p&q` by `&E` alone, and `>I` supplies the rest -- but the very cheapness is the point: `p>q` is supposed to say something conditional, and a true conjunction hands you one for free about any two truths whatsoever. Read as a *constraint on conditional logics* rather than a fact about `>`, the same schema is `CS` (Conjunctive Sufficiency), also called Strong Centering: it holds in Robert Stalnaker's system `C2` but fails in David Lewis's system `V`, precisely because Lewis's semantics allows several equally close worlds where `p` holds while `q` does not, whereas Stalnaker's uniqueness assumption collapses that gap the moment `p&q` is actually true. A conditional logic's stance on `CS` is a stance on whether nearness to the actual world is ever genuinely tied.

appearances.work: his conditional logic C2, in which Conjunctive Sufficiency (Strong Centering) is valid -- unlike David Lewis's rival system V

names: What makes Ross's paradox a paradox
entries.interest: `addition` (`p ⊢ p∨q`) is one line of `∨I` and never in question; this is the direction that fails, and the row's own gloss on why it earns a slot -- "the conclusion really is weaker" -- is exactly the fact that makes Ross's paradox a paradox rather than a triviality. If `(p∨q)⊃p` held, `∨I` would be reversible, `p∨q` would say no less than `p` itself, and "post the letter or burn it" would follow from *and entail* "post the letter" -- the imperative version of Addition would license nothing an agent hadn't already been told to do. It is precisely because the disjunction is *weaker* than either disjunct, witnessed here by `p=F,q=T`, that inferring it from `p` throws information away, and throwing information away is what makes the inference feel wrong when read as a command.

entries.interest: The valid `distribution` (`p&(q∨r) ⊃ (p&q)∨(p&r)`) moves `&` inside a disjunction that is already there; this row instead starts from `p∨(q&r)` and asks whether the `&` can simply be pulled out to cover the whole thing, `(p∨q)&r` -- and it cannot, because the `p`-disjunct of the premise carries no commitment to `r` at all. Both countermodels share exactly that shape: `p` true, `r` false, `q` either way. The row's own framing -- "forces the 8-row table rather than pattern-matching" -- is the pedagogical point: `distribution`'s validity trains a reflex to treat any `∨`/`&` reshuffling as free, and this is the reshuffling that reflex gets wrong.

english.gloss: It's Monday, or it's the weekend and sunny; so (it's Monday or it's the weekend) and it's sunny.

course.note: From §3.6's disjunction sweep (CLI-315) -- no course locus. `looks_like: distribution`: same two connectives reshuffled the other way, deliberately invalid where `distribution` is valid, and worth setting side by side.

nd.note: No derivation exists. Building `(p∨q)&r` needs `r` outright, and the `p`-disjunct of the premise gives no way to reach it -- there is no rule that manufactures `r` from `p` alone. The countermodels `p=T,q=T,r=F` and `p=T,q=F,r=F` are the two ways of taking that disjunct with `r` false.

entries.interest: `t_p` and `f_p` are deliberately opaque atoms proxying the metalinguistic claims "p is true" and "p is false" -- not `p` and `∼p` themselves, which the object language already handles on its own (see `excluded-middle`, a theorem regardless of what `p` says). Write bivalence itself as a schema over those two opaque atoms and it stops being a theorem: the one countermodel sets both false, which is exactly Shramko and Wansing's underdetermined value, the gap a logic like Kleene's K3 is built to hold open. Nothing in the bare schema connects `t_p` and `f_p` to a single valuation or to each other -- supplying that connection is what Convention T does (`t_p≡p, f_p≡∼p ⊢ t_p∨f_p` is valid, checked directly), and only once it is supplied does bivalence follow. Paired with `no-gluts`, its glut-side twin.

appearances.quote: the principle of bivalence taken as a metatheoretical principle, viz. that there exist only two distinct logical values

course.note: From the comprehensive sweep's §3.8 ("Truth values -- excluded middle versus bivalence, and Suszko's thesis") -- no course locus, not a set question. The row's own point is a level distinction: `p∨∼p` and `∼(p&∼p)` are theorems, and their metalinguistic shadows, written with opaque `t_p`/`f_p` atoms, are not.

nd.note: Assume `∼(t_p∨f_p)` and aim at `⊥`, the standard route into a disjunction goal with no premises to eliminate. That extracts `∼t_p` and `∼f_p` separately (the same case-and-collide move `de-morgan-disjunction` already uses), and there the derivation stops: nothing else names either atom, so nothing turns the pair into a contradiction. The open branch is exactly the countermodel, `t_p=F, f_p=F` -- the gap.

entries.interest: The mirror case: the one countermodel sets both `t_p` and `f_p` true, Priest's overdetermined value, the glut a paraconsistent logic like LP is built to hold open. `∼(p&∼p)`, non-contradiction, stays a theorem regardless of what `p` says (see `non-contradiction`); this is its own metalinguistic shadow, written over the same opaque `t_p`/`f_p` pair as `bivalence-schema`, and like its partner it fails for want of anything connecting the two atoms to a single valuation. Together the two open countermodels are exactly the gap and the glut: classical semantics rules both out, but not by deriving that exclusion from `p∨∼p` and `∼(p&∼p)` alone.
